title: Harsha slams Govt.’s India stance | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 24 November 2026 01:56
-     - 130

Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) MP Dr. Harsha de Silva yesterday accused the Government of lacking urgency on economic ties with India. He urged it to finalise the long-stalled Economic and Technology Cooperation Agreement (ETCA) and to rework the country’s ports strategy so that it complements, rather than competes with, India’s port expansion.

Speaking in Parliament, Dr. de Silva said India was not simply a trading partner. It was Sri Lanka’s largest trading partner, its second-largest export market as a single country, its largest source of tourists and one of its largest investors, as well as the fastest-growing large economy in the world. Sri Lanka’s economic and strategic future, and its goal of becoming the maritime and logistics hub of the Indian Ocean, were closely tied to India, he said.

He said roughly 60-70% of India’s transshipment cargo went to the Port of Colombo, which made India part of the economic infrastructure that sustained the port’s operations rather than just a market. He questioned whether India’s Vizhinjam port would compete with or complement Colombo. He also noted that MSC had recently bought 49% of Adani Vizhinjam Port Private Ltd for $ 1.4 billion.

Dr. de Silva said Sri Lanka had to decide how far it would liberalise trade in services. He asked whether the country would continue to protect “one or two or three big business houses” by keeping the Port of Colombo’s logistics services closed above a 40% equity ownership limit. An integrated logistics base would require equity ownership to be opened up not only in warehousing and logistics but also in shipping agency and freight forwarding, which he said was the model in India, Dubai and Singapore.

“If we want to really become the maritime and logistics hub of this ocean, you have to understand that what matters to the investor has to be what we are willing to offer. If not, forget the idea of becoming the maritime hub of the Indian Ocean,” he said.

Turning to trade agreements, Dr. de Silva noted that the free trade agreement with India had been signed under the Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga Government. He said the Minister had stated that it would be looked at again. The agreement had been reviewed repeatedly, he said, but neither the proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) nor the ETCA had materialised.

He said the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP) had vowed in Opposition never to allow the ETCA to be signed, and said he would table material he had downloaded from its website.

“Now, I know you all have changed. As a matter of fact, from what I see, you have changed 180 degrees. The anti-India sentiment has become a very pro-India sentiment, which we encourage and which we welcome,” Dr. de Silva said.

He questioned whether the Government’s prioritisation of India was “just grand rhetoric” or backed by a realistic plan. If it was serious, he said, it should understand and resolve the outstanding issues and sign the ETCA. He said the Government had appointed a committee but showed no urgency. He asked whether its members had the expertise to understand the problems Sri Lankan exporters faced in India over standards, certifications and other barriers.

“It is not about selling. It is about participating in a structured, integrated production engine,” he said, adding that the relationship was about manufacturing, services and logistics.

However, Dr. de Silva said India was not the be-all and end-all. China, the East and the West were also important partners, and each relationship, including those with the European Union and the United States, had to be handled on its own terms.

He criticised the Government for failing to appoint ambassadors to Washington, Beijing, Berlin and Ottawa, among other capitals, two years after the Minister took office. 

Dr. de Silva also called for foreign missions to be held to account for investment results. He noted that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs had launched an integrated mechanism with the Ministry of Industries and Trade in September 2025 to coordinate missions with trade and investment institutions, with identifying potential foreign investors among its objectives. He asked the Minister to table, for each mission, the number of qualified investors introduced to the Board of Investment (BOI), the foreign direct investment (FDI) actually realised, and the targets set and achieved. The Ministry’s 2024 report had claimed 75% achievement of its FDI promotion target, which he described as a very vague figure.

“It can no longer be the number of meetings or networking events. It has to actually deliver,” he said.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a $ 200 million loan to help Sri Lanka strengthen micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) by expanding access to inclusive finance, reducing credit information gaps, and building resilience to shocks.

The financing package consists of a $ 100 million policy-based loan to improve the financial ecosystem for MSMEs and a $ 100 million financial intermediation loan to expand access to investment loans for MSMEs, including $ 40 million for green loans.

“This program will help the Government of Sri Lanka build a stronger, more inclusive financial ecosystem that enables MSMEs to grow, innovate, and withstand economic shocks and disasters related to the changing climate,” said ADB Country Director for Sri Lanka Shannon Cowlin. “By improving access to finance—especially for women entrepreneurs—and expanding green financing, ADB is supporting Sri Lanka’s transition to a more inclusive, resilient, and sustainable financing ecosystem for MSMEs.”

MSMEs are crucial to Sri Lanka’s economy, contributing more than 52% of gross domestic product and 45% of overall employment. However, they continue to be constrained by limited access to finance, low levels of digitalisation, and vulnerability to shocks such as disasters related to the changing climate.

Building a strong and inclusive financial ecosystem for MSMEs and sector development program will address these challenges by expanding financial inclusion through enhanced digitalisation, improving equitable access to information for MSMEs, formalising institutional processes, and enhancing financial literacy. 

It will support legal reforms to establish the Microfinance and Credit Regulatory Authority, improve oversight and reduce predatory lending, strengthen credit information systems to reduce information gaps, expand credit guarantees, and advance digital financial infrastructure and consumer protection.

Credit lines will be provided by participating financial institutions to expand green financing for MSMEs engaged in environmentally sustainable investments and activities. The program will help MSMEs—at least 20% of which are owned or led by women—invest in measures to mitigate and adapt to shocks related to the changing climate. It will also support innovative financing mechanisms to help growth-stage SMEs access equity financing.

title: Sajith urges FTAs that deliver comparative advantage, ‘positive alignments’ with all nations | Daily FT
summary:

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa yesterday called on Sri Lanka to pursue free trade agreements (FTAs) that deliver comparative advantages to the country rather than FTAs for their own sake. He urged the Government to make economic diplomacy central to a more proactive foreign policy.

Speaking in Parliament, Premadasa said economic diplomacy should ensure that Sri Lanka’s economic objectives were achieved. 



He questioned to what extent the present Government had used it to secure gains for the country.

“It is of utmost importance that we promote free trade agreements. Not free trade agreements per se, I must say. We must ensure that we promote free trade agreements that accrue comparative advantages to our country,” he said.

Premadasa set out 12 pillars against which he said the success of any foreign policy should be judged. They included protecting national interests and national security, achieving economic goals through economic diplomacy, maintaining constructive relations with all nations, respecting international law, protecting Sri Lankans overseas, and making full use of the country’s geographical location.

Measured against those pillars, he said, the country had fallen short. He questioned to what extent Sri Lanka had used and sustainably exploited the 200 nautical miles of sea it is entitled to under the United Nations conventions on the Law of the Sea.

“I’m afraid if we look at those aspects, we as a country have not fully utilised our position in the global world, our international status, to ensure that we fulfil these objectives,” Premadasa said.

He said Sri Lanka’s geographical location was unique and could be used to achieve strategic goals, which could in turn translate into prosperity for its people. While using that location to its advantage, the country should work with all partners that would bring benefits to Sri Lankans, he said.

Premadasa rejected non-alignment as the guiding principle of foreign policy. Instead, he said, the Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) would seek positive alignments with as many nations as possible.

“I know there is this famous buzzword of being non-aligned. I would say the reverse. In fact, the Samagi Jana Balawegaya doctrine would be to have as many positive alignments with nation states, with members of the international world,” he said.

He said such relationships must contribute directly to the country’s economic recovery.

Premadasa said Sri Lanka could promote the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) and the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA). However, he said all except BIMSTEC had become extremely dormant, and he urged Sri Lanka to take the lead in promoting regional cooperation. He added that the country had a moral duty to protect and secure its maritime boundaries and resources.

On climate, he said sustainable development and climate action should not be confined to talk, press conferences and declarations. He said Sri Lanka should play a leading role in persuading nations to make concessions, noting that the COP 31 negotiations in Turkey were at an absolute standstill.

To achieve a coherent foreign policy, Premadasa urged External Affairs Minister Vijitha Herath to adopt a modern decision-making process, establish new structures and set up think tanks to provide sound policy inputs. He said the Opposition would support all initiatives that would benefit the country’s 22 million people and would not be swayed by political prejudice.

title: NCE renews call for clear timeline on Sri Lanka’s accession to Madrid System | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 24 November 2026 06:14
-     - 38

The National Chamber of Exporters of Sri Lanka (NCE) has warned that Sri Lanka’s accession to the World Intellectual Property Organisation’s (WIPO) Madrid System is still awaiting the completion of the required legislative amendments. 

The National Intellectual Property Office of Sri Lanka (NIPO) has reviewed the amended Bill and communicated the required corrections to the Legal Draftsman’s Department, and is awaiting the final Bill before it can be submitted to the Attorney General’s Department for legal clearance. No confirmed timeline has yet been provided for the country’s accession to the system.

The NCE has brought the matter to the attention of NIPO and the Trade, Commerce, Food Security and Co-operative Development Minister multiple times, highlighting the need for clarity on the remaining steps and a practical timeframe for completion. The Chamber has also offered to provide private-sector input to support the process.

According to the latest update, the accession process has reached an advanced stage. The Intellectual Property (Amendment) Bill, incorporating the provisions required for Sri Lanka’s accession to the Madrid Protocol, had been forwarded to the Trade, Commerce, Food Security and Co-operative Development Ministry Secretary. Following a review of the amended draft, observations submitted by NIPO had been incorporated, subject to clarifications on two sections identified by the Legal Draftsman.

The required corrections were communicated to the Legal Draftsman’s Department, with a request for the final Bill. Once the final Bill is received, the Ministry will submit it to the Attorney General’s Department for legal clearance, after which it will proceed through the standard legislative process in Parliament. Despite the lack of a definitive date at this stage, the process is moving forward.

“However, the delay has practical implications for businesses looking to register and protect their brands in overseas markets. At present, Sri Lankan companies have to apply separately in each country where they require trademark protection. The cost can vary considerably depending on the destination and the nature of the application,” the NCE said. 

Estimates gathered by the NCE from member companies indicate that registering a trademark in an individual overseas market can cost from a few hundred US dollars to several thousand US dollars. These estimates include official filing fees, professional charges and other associated expenses, with the final cost depending on the country and the brand.

The expense can increase when a business seeks protection in several markets or across different classes of goods and services. This can be especially difficult for small and medium-sized exporters that are building their brands overseas and have to account for the cost of registration in each market.

Sri Lanka’s accession to the Madrid System would provide a more straightforward route to international trademark registration. The system allows an eligible applicant to submit a single international application through the country’s own intellectual property office and request protection in any or all of the member countries. This replaces the need to submit separate applications to each participating country, while providing a centralised process for managing international registrations.

The reach of the system has also grown. WIPO’s Madrid System currently has 117 members covering 133 countries and representing more than 80% of global trade. In 2025, an estimated 64,150 international trademark applications were filed through the system, with Asia accounting for 25.6% of the total.

Once Sri Lanka joins, a business that is a national of, is domiciled in or has a business in the country, and has filed for or registered a trademark locally, would be able to use the system to request protection in the markets it selects. As new jurisdictions join, the geographical coverage of an existing international registration can also be expanded.

The system is especially significant to Sri Lankan businesses whose products and services are entering international markets under local brands. This includes exporters in sectors such as tea, apparel, spices, gems and jewellery, processed foods and IT services. As companies develop value-added products and build recognition in overseas markets, protecting their names and trademarks becomes an essential part of their export plans.

Without registration in a particular market, for instance, a business may face difficulties if another party registers the same or a similar brand there. Resolving such disputes can be costly and time-consuming, and may affect the local company’s ability to use its brand in that market. A more accessible international registration process would therefore be crucial to companies expanding into several export destinations.

Trademark protection is also part of the intellectual property environment that overseas investors consider when assessing a country for business and investment. Access to an established international registration system can provide greater clarity for foreign companies looking at partnerships, manufacturing operations, franchise arrangements and other commercial activities involving Sri Lankan businesses.

The NCE has been collecting cost information from member companies and consulting sectoral representatives to support its work on the issue. The Chamber considers Sri Lanka’s accession to the Madrid System relevant to the country’s larger export ambitions, especially as local businesses seek to build internationally recognised brands and increase the value of their products and services.

The outstanding legislative work is therefore a necessary step in making the system accessible to Sri Lankan businesses. The NCE has reiterated the need for a clear timeframe for its completion, so exporters can plan their trademark registration requirements with a better understanding of when the international system will be available through Sri Lanka.

The Government is moving to overhaul and consolidate Sri Lanka’s existing labour law framework through a proposed new legislative package covering employment conditions, workplace protections, social security and trade union rights.

The proposed reforms, being formulated by an expert committee appointed with Cabinet approval, aim to bring the country’s labour laws in line with the changing and future demands of the world of work, Labour Ministry officials told Members of Parliament at a special briefing held on 18 November.

The initiative seeks to establish a new legal framework by reviewing and consolidating the major labour laws currently in force, with the proposed reforms structured around four key areas; labour standards, occupational health and safety, industrial relations and disputes, and trade union rights.

The proposed framework is expected to address a broad range of employment-related provisions, including formalisation of employment contracts, working hours, leave entitlements, overtime, maternity protection, paternity leave and the prevention of violence and harassment in the workplace.

It will also seek to strengthen provisions governing part-time employment, social security benefits and the right of employees to a safe working environment, signalling a broader review of employment protections and workplace rights.

The Ministry has already published the four chapters of the proposed Labour Standards Bill drafted so far on its official website, inviting members of the public and relevant stakeholders to submit comments and proposals.

Officials said the views of trade unions, employers and employee representatives would also be considered in developing the proposed legislation, indicating that stakeholder consultation will form part of the law-making process.

The briefing was held under the patronage of Labour Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha who is also the Ministerial Consultative Committee on Labour Affairs Chairman. Labour Deputy Minister Mahinda Jayasinghe, MPs and Ministry officials also participated.

ITAK MP Shanakiyan Rasamanickam

Ilankai Tamil Arasu Katchi (ITAK) Parliamentary Group Leader MP Shanakiyan Rasamanickam has questioned the Government’s commitment to human rights and accountability. He said it was going ahead with two security-related Bills despite serious objections from the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka (HRCSL).

Speaking in Parliament, Rasamanickam asked how the Government could keep telling the international community that domestic mechanisms were enough to deliver justice and accountability while it disregarded the recommendations of its own independent Commission.

He said the HRCSL had written to the Minister of Justice and National Integration about the Prevention of Organised Crime Bill. The Commission identified provisions resembling those in the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), warned that the proposed law threatened fundamental rights and freedoms, and called for the Bill’s withdrawal. 

It had raised similar concerns about the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill, warning that provisions introduced under the pretext of protecting the State could seriously undermine citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms.

“How can the Government proceed with these Bills without addressing the concerns raised by its own Human Rights Commission? This is a serious issue that raises fundamental questions about the Government’s commitment to human rights and accountability,” Rasamanickam said.

He pointed out that whenever Sri Lanka’s human rights record was discussed at the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC), successive governments had maintained that accountability could be achieved through domestic mechanisms. He argued that the Government’s apparent unwillingness to act on the HRCSL’s recommendations called the credibility of those assurances into question.

“If the Government is unwilling to listen to its own independent Human Rights Commission, how can the Tamil people or the international community be expected to place confidence in domestic accountability mechanisms?” he asked.

Turning to the Northern and Eastern Provinces, Rasamanickam said long-standing problems of land occupation, restrictions on fundamental freedoms, intimidation and harassment remained unresolved. The continued failure to return land to its rightful owners was depriving affected communities of their fundamental rights and preventing them from rebuilding their lives, he said. 

Civilians, journalists and people advocating for justice and accountability also continued to face intimidation and harassment. He urged the HRCSL to investigate these matters thoroughly and said he was concerned that such allegations kept emerging under the present Government despite its promises of democratic reform and respect for fundamental rights.

On the Chemmani mass grave investigation, Rasamanickam responded to remarks the Minister of Justice made in Parliament about a report submitted by archaeologist Prof. Somadeva. The Minister had described the document as merely a report and indicated that the Court had taken a similar position. Rasamanickam said ITAK remained committed to pursuing justice through the judicial process. 

He noted that ITAK General Secretary President’s Counsel M. A. Sumanthiran had appeared before the Court in person and had submitted affidavits on behalf of individuals willing to undergo DNA testing, to help further investigations.

“We are pursuing justice for the victims of Chemmani through the Courts. We have no intention of engaging in cheap political theatrics,” he said.

He also criticised individuals who, he alleged, had collected money in connection with demonstrations organised during Maaveerar Day commemorations, and said his party would not engage in such practices. He also criticised a Minister representing the Northern Province for what he described as a lack of understanding of these matters. 

Rasamanickam noted that the HRCSL’s report on the Northern and Eastern Provinces had also addressed the Chemmani issue. He said justice for the victims and their families required credible investigations, forensic evidence and meaningful judicial action rather than political statements.

Rasamanickam also called on the Judicial Service Commission (JSC) to resolve an administrative problem in the Batticaloa District without further delay. Fines collected by the Police within the jurisdiction of the Valaichchenai Pradeshiya Sabha were being credited to another local authority, he said. 

The matter had been brought to the JSC’s attention and raised repeatedly with the Minister of Justice, but it had remained unresolved for about a year. The Minister had indicated that it required the JSC’s intervention. Rasamanickam also highlighted a shortage of staff in the Court Registrars’ Service, which he said was contributing to delays in judicial proceedings.

He urged the Election Commission to ensure Provincial Council elections are held at least in 2027. He noted that while the Commission had most recently conducted the Local Government elections, the provincial polls had been postponed for several years. The absence of elected Provincial Councils deprived people of their democratic right to representation at the provincial level, he said, and he urged the authorities to use the funds allocated for elections to hold the polls next year.

Rasamanickam welcomed the environmental work carried out under the Government’s Clean Sri Lanka program in several parts of the country, including the renovation of the Bambalapitiya Railway Station and the cleaning of its surroundings. However, he said coastal communities in the Batticaloa District faced serious environmental problems. 

Large quantities of beer bottles, medical vials and plastic waste were frequently washing ashore along the district’s coastline, much of it believed to come from vessels at sea rather than from coastal residents. He asked the Government to provide specialised beach-cleaning machinery to the district, noting that the Kaluwanchikudy Pradeshiya Sabha had also submitted a proposal for such machinery. He also called for adequate public toilet facilities in public places throughout the district.

He also called for the additional allowance paid to parliamentary employees to be reviewed and increased. At Rs. 750, it had remained unchanged for about 10 years despite the rising cost of living and the responsibilities these employees carry.

Concluding, Rasamanickam said the Government must show its commitment to human rights, democratic governance and accountability through concrete action rather than assurances given in Parliament or before international institutions.

“Respect for fundamental rights, accountability and the rule of law must begin with the Government itself,” he said.

Maldivian President Dr. Mohammed Muizzu

Maldivian President Dr. Mohammed Muizzu’s call for fairer climate finance at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, comes at a particularly relevant time for Sri Lanka. With Colombo still grappling with the aftermath of recent flooding and the country recovering from the devastation caused by Cyclone Ditwah, the growing cost of extreme weather is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. 

For Sri Lanka, the challenge is not only to protect lives, livelihoods and infrastructure from future disasters, but also to find ways of financing these efforts without adding further pressure to an already fragile economic recovery.

On the 6 November 2026, heavy rain brought parts of Colombo to a standstill. Roads disappeared beneath floodwater, motorists were stranded, shops struggled to protect their goods and sections of the National Hospital were inundated. For thousands of people trying to get home from work, run a business or reach essential services, the disruption was immediate. The flooding also exposed problems that have troubled the capital for years. Blocked canals, inadequate drainage, unauthorised construction and the steady loss of open spaces have made it increasingly difficult for rainwater to escape. Following the floods, the Colombo Municipal Council identified 60 locations requiring urgent intervention. For a shopkeeper whose stock has been damaged, or a worker who loses a day’s income because transport has stopped, these are not abstract infrastructure problems. They have real financial consequences. 

The events in Colombo provide a timely backdrop to the intervention made by Maldivian President Dr. Mohammed Muizzu at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey on the 11 November 2026. Dr. Muizzu questioned why countries highly vulnerable to climate impacts should be expected to borrow heavily to protect themselves against a crisis they have contributed relatively little to creating. 

“We cannot be expected to borrow our way out of a crisis we did little to create,” he told delegates. His appeal for more predictable grants and fairer international financing arrangements speaks directly to Sri Lanka’s circumstances. Having endured a severe economic crisis, the country must now find ways to protect its development gains against disasters that can erase years of investment in a matter of hours.

When the cost goes beyond the damage

The destruction caused by Cyclone Ditwah in November 2025 demonstrates how quickly a natural disaster can become a national economic problem. The World Bank’s initial rapid assessment estimated direct physical damage at $ 4.1 billion, equivalent to approximately 4% of Sri Lanka’s GDP. This figure did not include lost income, disrupted production or the full cost of recovery and reconstruction. In the transport sector alone, the World Bank subsequently estimated recovery requirements of $ 1.31 billion following extensive damage to provincial and rural roads and bridges. Behind these figures are communities whose everyday lives depend on functioning infrastructure.

Giving greater consideration to climate vulnerability in international financing decisions could help address this imbalance. Such recognition should not mean weaker accountability. Projects must still meet appropriate standards for procurement, environmental protection, technical design and long-term maintenance. The challenge is to make climate finance more accessible without compromising the quality of the investments it supports

When a rural road is washed away, a farmer may be unable to transport vegetables to market. A small business may lose customers because deliveries cannot get through. Children may miss school, while patients face longer journeys to reach medical care. The damage to the road is visible. The wider economic losses are often harder to measure. 

In September 2026, the World Bank approved $ 110 million to repair and reconstruct 600 kilometres of cyclone-damaged roads. The project includes improved drainage, landslide protection and updated engineering standards to help the infrastructure withstand future extreme weather. This approach recognises that simply restoring what existed before a disaster may leave communities exposed to the same risks. Although the precise contribution of climate change to Cyclone Ditwah remains uncertain, rising global temperatures can intensify heavy rainfall associated with severe storms. For Sri Lanka, where floods and landslides already cause substantial damage, building greater resilience is becoming an essential part of development planning.

Why prevention deserves greater financial support

One of the strongest points in Dr. Muizzu’s argument concerns how the international financial system values investments that prevent future losses. A renewable energy project can earn revenue by selling electricity. A flood protection scheme strengthened embankment or improved drainage network generally does not generate income in the same way. Yet the benefits can be considerable. 

Consider Colombo’s recent flooding. Better drainage, properly maintained canals, and protected water-retention areas could reduce the disruption caused by intense rainfall. Businesses would be less likely to lose trading days, households would face fewer repair bills and public services could continue operating. The value of these investments lies in the damage they help avoid. That creates a financing challenge. 

Governments are often expected to borrow for infrastructure projects even when the benefits are widely shared and cannot be recovered through user charges. For countries already managing substantial debt obligations, this can make essential adaptation investments difficult to finance. 

Dr. Muizzu’s call for greater grant support is therefore particularly relevant to projects that protect public welfare without generating direct commercial returns. Concessional loans, with affordable interest rates and long repayment periods, can also play a useful role where borrowing remains sustainable. Private investment may be appropriate for projects capable of generating reliable revenue. What matters is choosing financing arrangements suited to the project, rather than treating all climate investments as commercial opportunities.

Different countries, familiar concerns

The Maldives faces an especially difficult future because of its geography. At COP31, Dr. Muizzu noted that approximately 80% of Maldivian islands stand less than one metre above sea level, while nearly half the population lives within 100 metres of the coastline. Protecting shorelines is consequently central to the country’s economic security and the future of its communities. Earlier this year, Dr. Muizzu reported that six coastal protection projects had been completed in 2025, with another 62 at various stages of implementation.

World Leaders at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey

Sri Lanka’s circumstances are different, but coastal communities face their own pressures. Around a quarter of the population lives within one kilometre of the coastline. Fishing settlements, tourism facilities, agricultural land and freshwater supplies are exposed to coastal erosion, flooding and saltwater intrusion. For a fishing family, the loss of a landing site or damage to a home can threaten a livelihood built over generations. For coastal businesses, repeated flooding can make investment and recovery increasingly difficult. The concern is not only about protecting physical assets. It is also about preserving communities and the economic activities that sustain them.

The widening gap in climate finance

The scale of the global adaptation challenge adds urgency to Dr. Muizzu’s appeal. According to the United Nations Environment Program’s 2026 Adaptation Gap Report, developing countries will require an estimated $ 305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035. Even if the COP30 aspiration to triple international public adaptation finance by that year is achieved, UNEP estimates that the resulting funding would meet only 20% to 29% of developing countries’ needs. This leaves governments facing difficult choices about which investments to prioritise and which risks they can afford to address. 

It also highlights the need to distinguish between different forms of climate finance. Mitigation funding supports efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Adaptation finance helps communities prepare for and manage climate impacts. Loss and damage financing addresses harm that cannot be avoided. All three are necessary, but progress in reducing emissions does not remove the need to protect people already experiencing environmental threats. 

For Sri Lanka, the immediate challenge is particularly visible in damaged roads, flood-prone neighbourhoods, vulnerable coastal settlements and communities exposed to landslides.

Getting the money to where it is needed

Even when international climate funds are available, securing support is not always straightforward. Funding applications require detailed project proposals, feasibility studies, technical assessments and financial planning. Institutions must demonstrate that projects are properly designed, environmentally sound and capable of delivering lasting benefits. These requirements are important, but preparing credible proposals takes time, money and specialist expertise. Sri Lanka has taken steps to improve its access to international climate finance. 

DFCC Bank has been accredited to seek funding directly from the Green Climate Fund since 2023. The Maldives achieved a similar milestone in October 2026, when Maldives Finance and Leasing Company became its first nationally accredited institution. Such accreditation allows national institutions to submit funding proposals without depending entirely on international intermediaries. It can also strengthen local involvement in deciding which projects deserve priority. 

However, accreditation does not guarantee approval. This is why technical assistance for project preparation deserves greater attention. A community may urgently need flood protection, but without the institutional capacity to develop a convincing proposal, that need may never translate into an approved investment. Sri Lanka’s National Climate Finance Strategy for 2025 to 2030 offers a framework for addressing some of these challenges. 

Developed with support from UNDP and the United Kingdom, the strategy seeks to incorporate climate priorities into fiscal planning and investment decisions while identifying additional sources of finance. Its success will depend on how effectively national priorities are translated into practical projects, supported by coordination between Government agencies, financial institutions and development partners.

Looking beyond national income

Dr. Muizzu has also questioned the reliance on income indicators when determining countries’ eligibility for concessional financing. Speaking at COP31 on the 12 November 2026, he argued that income alone does not adequately reflect the vulnerabilities facing small states such as the Maldives. 

The concern has relevance for Sri Lanka. A country’s income classification may indicate its broad level of economic development, but it says relatively little about the damage a major flood, cyclone or landslide could cause. Nor does it fully reflect the pressure that repeated disasters place on public budgets. A country may be making progress in rebuilding its economy while remaining highly exposed to events capable of reversing those gains. 

Giving greater consideration to climate vulnerability in international financing decisions could help address this imbalance. Such recognition should not mean weaker accountability. Projects must still meet appropriate standards for procurement, environmental protection, technical design and long-term maintenance. The challenge is to make climate finance more accessible without compromising the quality of the investments it supports.

Preparedness can make the difference

Colombo’s recent floods also underline the importance of measures that do not necessarily require large construction projects. Timely warnings, reliable communication and clear emergency procedures can help people protect themselves and their belongings before conditions deteriorate. At COP31, Dr. Muizzu highlighted improved forecasting and community preparedness as essential components of climate resilience. Sri Lanka is taking steps in this direction. 

In November, an EU-supported initiative was announced to pilot disaster preparedness measures in Badulla and Matara. The program will work with local authorities, schools and communities to improve warning communication, prepare response plans and conduct simulation exercises. These measures can be especially valuable in areas where residents have limited time to respond to flash floods or landslides. An early warning is useful only when it reaches people in time and they know what action to take. Equally important is maintaining existing infrastructure. Colombo’s flooding demonstrated how blocked waterways and weaknesses in urban planning can worsen the effects of intense rainfall. Addressing such problems requires sustained attention, not only emergency clean-up operations after each disaster.

What this means for Sri Lanka

Dr. Muizzu’s appeal carries an important message for Sri Lanka as it seeks to strengthen climate resilience while safeguarding its economic recovery. Rebuilding after Cyclone Ditwah, improving Colombo’s flood management and protecting vulnerable coastal communities will require both international support and sound domestic planning. Better land-use policies, regular infrastructure maintenance and stronger institutional coordination are equally essential to reducing future losses. 

Sri Lanka must also make a stronger case for climate financing that recognises the wider economic and social benefits of adaptation, supported by an appropriate mix of grants, concessional loans and investment. While the Maldives faces the threat of rising seas, Sri Lanka must contend with recurring floods, damaged infrastructure and disrupted livelihoods. Both countries share an interest in financing arrangements that reflect their vulnerabilities. Ultimately, the success of climate finance should be measured not merely by funds mobilised, but by the communities, livelihoods and development gains it helps protect.

title: AKD, take that first step — The journey from which  there is no return | Daily FT
summary:

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

“If no one responds to your call, then go your own way alone.”

~Rabindranath Tagore,

By Vishwamithra

AKD, take that first step. Take it with the courage of a man who knows that history does not always announce the hour of its arrival. Sometimes it comes silently, without ceremony, without the thunder of drums or the applause of assembled multitudes. Sometimes it arrives disguised as uncertainty, demanding of one solitary individual the courage to venture where generations before him feared to tread.

Take that first step, AKD. For the road ahead is not one upon which the timid may travel, nor one from which the determined may return unchanged.

You may not recognize the landscape into which you are entering. Its mountains may appear unfamiliar, its valleys treacherous, its pathways concealed beneath the accumulated dust of centuries. The comforting landmarks of yesterday may disappear behind you. Those who once walked beside you may hesitate at the threshold, and those who await you beyond it may speak in unfamiliar voices, carrying unfamiliar dreams.

Yet do not mistake unfamiliarity for hostility, nor hesitation for betrayal.

For somewhere beyond the boundaries of party, class, caste, creed and ethnicity, there are men and women who have waited all their lives for this journey to begin. They may never have sung your songs, carried your banners or embraced your political philosophy. They may have opposed you yesterday and may question you tomorrow. But in the deepest chambers of their conscience, they too have heard the same ancient summons.

It is the summons of a nation yearning to become worthy of its own people.

For two thousand five hundred years, within the womb of Mother Lanka, there has dwelt a promise not yet fulfilled. Not a promise belonging to any single race, religion or dynasty, but one carried in the silent endurance of generations: the promise that this island, blessed with beauty and burdened with history, might one day become a land in which dignity is not purchased by privilege, justice is not determined by power, and opportunity is not inherited through blood.

That promise has survived the splendor of kingdoms and the ruin of empires. It has survived foreign conquest, colonial subjugation, communal suspicion, political betrayal and the bitter tragedies of civil conflict. It has lived in the calloused hands of the farmer, the weary eyes of the plantation worker, the patient endurance of the fisherman, the uncelebrated sacrifices of the teacher and the quiet desperation of the mother who sends her child across oceans in search of a future denied at home.

The task before you is not to become another celebrated occupant of the presidential chair. It is to help make that chair less powerful than the institutions of the Republic, less important than the rights of its citizens, and less enduring than the principles by which the country must be governed. Let that be the measure of your achievement. For Mother Lanka has waited long enough

It has lived in the sorrow of the North and the East, in the frustrations of the South, in the neglected villages of the dry zone and the crowded streets of Colombo. It has waited in every home where hope was repeatedly born, repeatedly betrayed, yet never entirely extinguished.

And now, perhaps, the hour has arrived when that ancient promise demands more than another speech, another election, another government or another procession of triumphant politicians.

It demands transformation.

Not merely a change of rulers, but a change in the very meaning of rule.

Not merely the punishment of yesterday’s wrongdoers, but the creation of a tomorrow in which wrongdoing can no longer find comfortable sanctuary.

Not merely the redistribution of political power, but the restoration of moral purpose to public life.

AKD, your greatest companions on this journey may not be those who applauded you most loudly at the beginning. They may be those who challenge your assumptions, question your certainties and insist that the dream of a new Sri Lanka must be larger than the ideology of any single movement.

Welcome them.

For a nation’s rebirth cannot be accomplished by the faithful alone. It requires the courage of former adversaries, the wisdom of dissenters, the imagination of the young and the experience of those who have witnessed both the triumphs and the failures of generations past.

Let the Tamil mother who still waits for answers, the Muslim citizen who seeks security without suspicion, the Sinhala villager who demands a fair chance in life, and the young professional who wonders whether to remain in the country of his birth all recognize themselves in the future you seek to build.

Let no citizen be asked to surrender an identity in order to claim a place in the nation.

And remember: the journey is irreversible not because one leader must remain forever in power, but because a people, once awakened to their own dignity, must never again be persuaded to surrender it.

There will be dark mornings. There will be betrayal and disappointment. There will be moments when the burden of expectation weighs more heavily than the machinery of government itself. The applause of the multitude may fade, and the solitude of leadership may become almost unbearable.

But history has never reserved its finest pages for those who chose comfort over conviction.

The task before you is not to become another celebrated occupant of the presidential chair. It is to help make that chair less powerful than the institutions of the Republic, less important than the rights of its citizens, and less enduring than the principles by which the country must be governed.

Let that be the measure of your achievement.

For Mother Lanka has waited long enough.

She has buried too many sons, mourned too many daughters, watched too many promises dissolve into the polluted waters of political expediency. Her soil has absorbed the tears of the innocent and the blood of the forgotten. Her children have inherited not merely the glory of an ancient civilization but the unresolved wounds of a modern nation.

She does not ask for another savior.

She asks for a generation courageous enough to make saviors unnecessary.

So, take that first step, AKD.

Take it not as the leader of a victorious party, but as the temporary custodian of a permanent national aspiration.

Take it knowing that those who begin the journey may not live to witness its destination; that the seeds planted today may blossom beneath skies unseen by their planters; that the noblest victories of public life are often those for which no individual can claim exclusive credit.

And when the familiar voices grow faint, when the road bends beyond the horizon, when yesterday’s certainties no longer illuminate tomorrow’s choices, remember that the true compass of this odyssey is neither party doctrine nor personal popularity.

It is the conscience of the people.

For somewhere in the depths of this ancient island, beneath the ruins of abandoned promises and the weight of unfulfilled dreams, the heartbeat of a different Sri Lanka can still be heard.

It is calling.

Not for a king. Not for a conqueror. Not for another name to be carved upon the monuments of political vanity.

It is calling for justice. For reconciliation. For decency. For a republic in which the humblest citizen may stand upright without fear before the mightiest institution of the State.

AKD, take that first step.

And let it be the first step of a nation that has finally decided never again to walk backwards.

title: Friends with all, subservient to none: Why Sri Lanka must guard its national interest | Daily FT
