There was a time when Sri Lanka stood taller in the world than its size or its wealth would suggest. Under the late Sirimavo Bandaranaike, this country practiced what I believe was the finest non-aligned foreign policy in our history. The idea of the Indian Ocean as a zone of peace was first raised by Sri Lanka at the Non-Aligned summit in Cairo in 1964. In 1971, it was Sri Lanka, later joined by Tanzania, that took the proposal to the United Nations, and on 16 December that year the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2832, declaring the Indian Ocean a Zone of Peace. In August 1976, Colombo hosted the Fifth Summit of the Non-Aligned Movement, welcoming leaders from across Asia, Africa and Latin America, and Mrs. Bandaranaike assumed the chair of the Movement. A small island helped to set the agenda for the great powers.

That was not luck. It was the product of three qualities: clarity, consistency and credibility. We knew who we were, we said the same thing to every capital, and we were believed. As our country faces one of the most complicated external environments in its modern history – with a war in the Middle East spilling into our waters, volatile trade policy in our largest market and intense competition for influence in our ports – those three qualities are worth recalling.

Foreign policy is not domestic politics

Foreign policy is unlike any other area of government. In domestic policy, a government can experiment, make a mistake and correct it at the next Budget. In foreign policy, a careless word, a hasty decision or a single port call can follow a nation for a generation. Foreign policy is not something to be played with for political applause at home.

Every country, large or small, has economic, political and security interests. Those who deal with us pursue theirs, and they do so without apology. Our task is to pursue ours with the same seriousness, but with a clear understanding of who we are, what our real strength is and where we stand. That means building a foreign policy that survives changes of government: one that is debated in Parliament, understood by the public and applied consistently by every ministry, so that our partners know what to expect from Sri Lanka regardless of who sits in office.

Sri Lanka as geopolitical turf

During the Cold War, the rivalry between the superpowers was largely conducted directly between them. Since then, geopolitics has changed. The contest is no longer fought mainly between the great powers themselves; it is fought in other countries: in their ports, their sea lanes, their infrastructure, their debts and their politics. Sri Lanka, sitting beside some of the busiest shipping lanes in the Indian Ocean, has become geopolitical turf. We must be mindful of that every single day.

We have learnt this the hard way. Many will remember 4 June 1987. Shortly after our Navy had turned back a flotilla of boats carrying supplies, parippu and other provisions were dropped from the air over Jaffna, and we were powerless to prevent it. Within weeks, the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord had been signed. We will remember, too, that in the years before that, those who took up arms against this State received training on foreign soil. I do not raise these matters to reopen old wounds with a neighbour with whom our relations today are close and valued. I raise them as lessons. When the interests of larger nations are engaged, a small nation must know its actual strength, and it must ask itself honestly whether it can take other countries on in the global arena.

The Iranian vessels: humanity and neutrality

This brings me to the events of this year. On 4 March, a United States submarine torpedoed the Iranian frigate IRIS Dena in international waters off Galle, as it was returning home from a naval exercise hosted by India. The ship had around 180 people on board. Responding to its distress call, the Sri Lanka Navy, supported by the Sri Lanka Air Force, rescued 32 survivors and recovered 87 bodies. The next day, a second Iranian naval vessel, IRIS Bushehr, reported engine trouble and sought assistance; more than 200 of its crew were brought ashore and the ship was placed under Sri Lankan control. Last month, around 40 Iranian sailors from tankers stranded off our southern coast by the naval blockade in the Gulf, many of them in urgent need of medical care, were brought ashore through Galle for treatment and then sent home.

We cannot leave our export earnings so heavily dependent on a handful of markets, however friendly. Trade agreements with emerging markets in Asia, the Middle East and Africa must be pursued with urgency, and our exporters, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, must be given the market intelligence, finance and diplomatic support to reach them. Our missions abroad should be judged, in part, by the new markets they open. That, too, is foreign policy

Let me be clear: Sri Lanka must never compromise on its humanitarian and human rights obligations. A sailor in distress is a human being first; his nationality comes second. International maritime law requires us to render assistance, and our own values, rooted in every one of our faiths, demand it. The President was right to say that every life is as precious as our own. I commend the Sri Lanka Navy, the Air Force, the doctors and nurses in Galle and Colombo, and everyone who responded so swiftly and professionally.

But humanitarian duty must go hand in hand with careful diplomacy. We must act transparently and through established international procedures, so that no one can say that Sri Lanka has taken sides in a war that is not ours. Parliament and the public deserve a clear account of the rules we are applying - who may enter our waters, on what terms, for how long, and what becomes of a vessel once it is in our custody. Neutrality is not silence, and it is not indifference. It is a principled position, and it must be explained clearly and consistently to all our partners, East and West alike. A small country that is seen to be neutral in word but partisan in deed loses the trust of everyone.

Trade, investment and the IMF: A delicate balance

Nowhere is this balance more important than in our economy. Consider the facts. Our exports go primarily to the West. The United States alone is our largest single export market, taking more than a fifth of our merchandise exports, and together with the European Union it accounts for nearly half of all we sell abroad; add the United Kingdom, and it is more than half. Apparel dominates our shipments to America, and the industry employs more than 300,000 workers directly, many of them women from our rural villages.

When tariffs are pushed up in Washington, it is our apparel workers in Katunayake, in Biyagama and in our villages who feel it first. Over the past two years, we have watched the duty on our goods swing wildly. In April 2025, 44% reciprocal tariff was announced on Sri Lankan exports; it was later cut to 30% and then to 20%. In February this year, the United States Supreme Court struck down the legal basis for those tariffs, and a temporary 10 per cent duty was imposed in their place. In July, a new regime set our rate at 10%, sparing us a higher bracket for now. Our exporters have lived with every twist of that uncertainty, and each adverse shift has pushed our economy downhill. Planning a factory, a production line or a season’s orders in such conditions is extraordinarily difficult, and it is the worker on the factory floor who carries the risk.

At the same time, China is a key source of foreign direct investment for this country. The Colombo Port City and the proposed $ 3.7 billion Sinopec oil refinery at Hambantota – described, when it was signed in January 2025, as the largest foreign direct investment in our history – are only the most visible examples. Much of that investment is meant to produce goods and services that we will sell abroad, including to the West. So we invest with one side and earn from the other. It is a complex scenario, and it cannot be managed with slogans. It requires skill, patience and a steady hand, and it requires us to ensure that every major investment is transparent, commercially sound and consistent with our sovereignty and our neutrality.

When the present Government assumed office, there was considerable concern that it would abandon the IMF program, and that it would engage only with the East and ignore the West. In fairness, that has not happened. The Government has continued with the program agreed in March 2023; the IMF Executive Board completed the combined fifth and sixth reviews in May this year, and staff reached agreement on the seventh review in October. The Government has engaged Washington on tariffs and Beijing on investment, and has, so far, managed to strike a balance. Credit must be given where it is due.

A word of caution, however. Remaining within the program is one thing; being ruled by the dictates of the IMF is quite another. The program is a means to recovery, not a substitute for our own economic policy. As Parliament debates the 2027 Budget, on which the next IMF tranche depends, the pensioner, the small trader and the daily-wage earner must see that the decisions taken in their name are made here, by our own Parliament, for their benefit, and that the burden of reform is shared fairly.

We must also diversify. We cannot leave our export earnings so heavily dependent on a handful of markets, however friendly. Trade agreements with emerging markets in Asia, the Middle East and Africa must be pursued with urgency, and our exporters, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, must be given the market intelligence, finance and diplomatic support to reach them. Our missions abroad should be judged, in part, by the new markets they open. That, too, is foreign policy.

Empty chairs in Washington and Beijing

Yet all of this balancing rests on something that, at present, we lack, our own ambassadors in the two capitals that matter most to us. Sri Lanka’s ambassadorial posts in Washington DC and in Beijing both stand vacant. Our Ambassador to China took formal leave of the Chinese Foreign Ministry in April, and our Ambassador to the United States ended his term and returned home in July. In August, by contrast, both the United States and China sent new ambassadors to Colombo, and each presented credentials to the President on the same day, 25 August. They are here, in our capital, advancing the interests of their countries, as they are entitled to do. We have no one of equal rank in theirs.

Some foreign nationals have arrived in Sri Lanka and taken jobs that are meant for our own citizens. Some have set up businesses, including guesthouses, surf schools, cafés and restaurants, and some of these establishments do not even welcome locals. In our own country, Sri Lankans are being made to feel unwelcome in places run by visitors. How can this happen? Who issued the approvals? Who is checking the visas? Who is collecting the taxes?

This is not a question of protocol. An ambassador is not a ceremonial figure. He or she is the voice of the Head of State in a foreign capital, with access to ministers, legislators and decision-makers that no chargé d’affaires, however able, can command. Consider what is at stake. In Washington, the tariff on our goods has been set and reset four times in little more than a year, and every change has been decided in rooms where Sri Lanka needed to be heard. In Beijing, the largest investment in our history is still to be built, and the terms on which it proceeds will shape our economy for decades. And in both capitals, our handling of the Iranian vessels is being watched closely and judged. These are precisely the moments when a small country must speak through its most senior representative, not wait for messages to be relayed.

Our business community has already sounded the alarm. In August, the BRICS Chamber of Commerce (Sri Lanka) wrote to the President and the Minister of Foreign Affairs about the vacancies in both the United States and China, urging the appointment of envoys with proven diplomatic skill and commercial standing. Our apparel exporters, our investors and the hundreds of thousands of workers who depend on them cannot afford to have Sri Lanka’s case presented by default.

I therefore urge the Government to nominate ambassadors to Washington and Beijing without further delay, and to place those names before the Committee on High Posts at the earliest opportunity. Those chosen must be selected on merit – for their experience, their judgement and their understanding of trade and investment – not as a reward for political loyalty. And they should be appointed together. Filling both posts at the same time would itself send a message, East and West alike, that Sri Lanka gives equal weight to both relationships. An empty embassy in one capital is a misfortune; empty embassies in both, for months on end, risk being read as indifference, and that is a message no non-aligned nation can afford to send.

Let me also be clear that we welcome every tourist. Visitors who respect our laws, our culture and our communities are our honoured guests. Genuine foreign investors who come through the proper channels, create jobs for Sri Lankans and pay their taxes are welcome too. This is not about any nationality, and it must never become so. It is about the rule of law

Tourism must serve the people of Sri Lanka

As a former Deputy Minister of Tourism, I have watched with pride as our tourism industry has recovered from the Easter Sunday attacks, the pandemic and the economic crisis. Last year, Sri Lanka welcomed 2,362,521 tourists, the highest number in our history, surpassing the previous record set in 2018. Tourism feeds families in every corner of this island: the three-wheeler driver, the cook, the guide, the fisherman who supplies the beach restaurant. But I am deeply concerned about what is happening in some of our best-known resorts.

Some foreign nationals have arrived in Sri Lanka and taken jobs that are meant for our own citizens. Some have set up businesses, including guesthouses, surf schools, cafés and restaurants, and some of these establishments do not even welcome locals. In our own country, Sri Lankans are being made to feel unwelcome in places run by visitors. How can this happen? Who issued the approvals? Who is checking the visas? Who is collecting the taxes?

The law is clear - those who come on tourist visas are not permitted to do business here. Yet in Arugam Bay, in Weligama, in Hikkaduwa and elsewhere, such businesses continue, often through proxy local partners. Our registered hoteliers and tour operators pay their taxes, follow the regulations and train local staff. These unregulated operators do none of that, and they undercut our own people. They also deprive the Treasury of revenue at a time when every rupee counts, and they damage the reputation of destinations that our own entrepreneurs have spent decades building.

I acknowledge that the authorities have acted. According to the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority, 75 foreign nationals were arrested and 15 deported last year for doing business while on tourist visas. But treating these cases merely as individual visa violations is not enough. The problem is structural, and it requires a structural response. Other destinations in our region have faced the same challenge and have learnt that occasional raids, without proper registration, licensing and tax enforcement, simply move the problem from one beach to the next.

(The author is a President’s Counsel, a Member of Parliament, former Minister of Sports and former Deputy Minister of Tourism)

Let me also be clear that we welcome every tourist. Visitors who respect our laws, our culture and our communities are our honoured guests. Genuine foreign investors who come through the proper channels, create jobs for Sri Lankans and pay their taxes are welcome too. This is not about any nationality, and it must never become so. It is about the rule of law. The unregulated way in which some of these businesses operate is a direct threat to a vibrant and inclusive tourism industry – an industry that must, above all, benefit the people of Sri Lanka.

I have therefore called upon the Government to take four steps:

1. Carry out a comprehensive, district-by-district audit of foreign-run tourism businesses, so that we know the true scale of the problem.

2. Close the proxy-ownership loopholes and strengthen joint enforcement by the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority, the Department of Immigration and Emigration and the Police.

3. Introduce clear and transparent rules for foreigners who genuinely wish to invest or work in tourism, so that the honest are welcomed and the dishonest are removed.

4. Make it unlawful for any tourism establishment in Sri Lanka to refuse service to Sri Lankans on the ground of their nationality.

Respected by all, dominated by none

The threads of this argument run together. A warship in distress, a tariff in Washington, an investment from Beijing and a café in Arugam Bay may seem to be unrelated matters. They are not. Each tests whether we are willing to put the interests of Sri Lanka and its people first – calmly, consistently and without fear. Each demands that we know our strength, respect our obligations and speak with one voice. And that voice must be heard where it matters most: we cannot speak with one voice in Washington and Beijing if there is no one there to speak for us.

Mrs. Bandaranaike showed us that a small country can be respected by all and dominated by none, if it knows its strength, acts with consistency and speaks with one voice. Friends with all, subservient to none. That must be our foreign policy, our economic policy and our tourism policy.

title: Sri Lanka’s trade and diplomatic ties under fresh scrutiny post US midterm election | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 24 November 2026 00:00
-     - 37

I hope that as the most important and most powerful superpower of the world, America does discover the geography of South Asia, does discover the geography of the Indian Ocean and does discover the importance of a genuine mutually beneficial friendship with India 

- Former Indian Minister of State for External Affairs 

M.J. Akbar

It is important for the Government to appoint a new Ambassador to Washington, who is prepared to represent its interests to engage with many of the new members of Congress, a number of whom know very little about Sri Lanka

 - Former US Ambassador to Sri Lanka Robert O. Blake

The US did not provide us with offensive weapons, but it did provide intelligence, the war would probably have continued for many more years 

- Former Foreign Secretary and Sri Lankan Ambassador to the US Ravinatha Aryasinha

By Shanika Sriyananda 

The Americans has delivered its verdict at the US midterm elections. According to political analysts with Democrats gaining control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, President Donald Trump is likely to face influences in his policy approaches in different sectors including trade, foreign policy, security and the relationship with the Global South. 

The changing political landscape in the US indicates significant implications for Sri Lanka for its relationship with the US, which is the largest export partner, accounting for nearly a quarter of the country’s exports. 

At the webinar organised by the Pathfinder Foundation titled ‘America Votes, South Asia Adjusts: Implications for Sri Lanka and the Region’ former diplomates and policy experts looked into the implications of Washington’s political shift for South Asia, with trade access, human rights, international relations and regional security as key concerns

“For Sri Lanka and its neighbours, the task is not simply to understand Washington’s intentions but also to anticipate how its decisions may affect our economies, security and external relationships. Should we expect a change in American foreign policy?  And are we in South Asia prepared to respond?” commencing the discussion Pathfinder Foundation Chairman Ambassador (Retd.) Bernard Goonetilleke, who moderated the session, raised the question.

Referring to possible foreign relations changes of the US with South Asia and China’s growing influence in South Asia and the Indian Ocean, Goonatileke said the question was whether a change in Washington would give regional countries more room to pursue their interests or bring new pressures to choose sides.

“The Indian Ocean also deserves particular attention. Securing maritime trade routes and chokepoints, maritime security, freedom of navigation, port infrastructure and undersea communications are becoming increasingly important”, he said adding that those matters have direct implications for Sri Lanka and the wider Indian Ocean region.

The speakers highlighted the possible implications of the changing political balance in Washington for US relations with India, Pakistan, China and other South Asian countries, while highlighting the economic and strategic considerations facing Sri Lanka.

India cannot be sidelined in regional security

Former Indian Minister of State for External Affairs M.J. Akbar stressed that the United States could not overlook India’s strategic importance in maintaining security and stability in West Asia, South Asia and the wider Indo-Pacific.

Akbar is a veteran journalist and a politicians who has written several books, including ‘The Past and Future of Pakistan’.  

He said India’s role in the changing geopolitical landscape would become increasingly significant, particularly as conflicts stretching from Ukraine to West Asia and the Indian Ocean became more interconnected.

Questioning the Trump administration’s apparent shift away from the Indo-Pacific framework, Akbar asked whether Washington could afford to exclude India from the region’s security architecture.

“Can you remove India from the architecture of security and stability of West Asia, of the Indo-Pacific and of Asia?” he asked.

Akbar emphasised that India’s independent foreign policy should not be mistaken for opposition to international partnerships or cooperation with the United States.

“Independence is not a contrarian position. It is a position in which we offer partnership for a world order but through mutual cooperation, through an understanding of bilateral and even multilateral interests,” he said.  

Describing India as a pivotal power in South Asia and Asia, Akbar said the country would become an increasingly influential force in regional and international affairs.

“India is a pivotal power in South Asia, it is a pivotal power in Asia and it will become an increasingly powerful force for the good of the region and for the good of the world,” he said.

“What I have described as the war of the five seas, searching for the sixth. The war in Ukraine began with Crimea in 2014. The five seas are the Mediterranean, Caspian, Red, Black and Arabian seas, with the conflict almost reaching the sixth sea – the Indian Ocean,” he said giving the focus to the Indian Ocean.

He identified Taiwan and the Malacca Strait as important flashpoints in the evolving US-China strategic rivalry and stressed the importance of India’s naval presence in the region.

Akbar also cautioned that the election outcome could influence Washington’s approach towards West Asia, including its policy on Iran, and warned of the possibility of renewed military escalation. 

“There is a possibility that, because he does not want to be entre history books as a loser, he could actually reignite the conflict,” he said. 

He also raised questions about the future of US-India relations and the implications of Washington’s evolving approach to the Indo-Pacific, stressing that India’s strategic interests and regional role would remain important considerations for the United States.

Concluding his remarks, he urged the United States to recognise the strategic importance of South Asia and the Indian Ocean and the need for a mutually beneficial relationship with India. 

“I do hope that as the most important and most powerful superpower of the world, America does discover the geography of South Asia, does discover the geography of the Indian Ocean and does discover the importance of a genuine mutually beneficial friendship with India,” he said.

Repealing PTA

Former US Ambassador to Sri Lanka Robert O. Blake focused on the implications of the election results for Sri Lanka, particularly the potential influence of the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress on the Trump administration’s policies.

He identified US tariff policies and the possible renewal of the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) as two important issues for Sri Lanka, given the significance of the American market to the country’s exports.

“The U.S. remains Sri Lanka’s most important export market,” he, who is the Senior Managing Director at McLarty Associates, where he leads the Climate and Sustainability and Southeast Asia practices, said.

Blake noted that Democrats would have opportunities to challenge some of President Donald Trump’s tariff measures when they assume control of the House of Representatives and Senate in January 2027.

However, cautioning against expecting a complete reversal of the existing tariff, said that he would not assume that Democrats would automatically seek to repeal them. “ It is worth remembering that when President Biden succeeded the first Trump administration, he retained most of the trade measures introduced during Trump’s first term,” he recalled.

Ambassador Blake said that the GSP scheme, which provides duty-free access to the US market for thousands of products from designated developing countries, including Sri Lanka, had lapsed in 2020.

He said its renewal was unlikely to be an immediate priority for the incoming Congress. However, if Democrats decided to revive the program, they could seek stronger provisions relating to workers’ rights, environmental protection and human rights.

“The latter in particular could bring renewed scrutiny on Sri Lanka,” he warned.

Blake stressed that Sri Lanka needed to strengthen its engagement with the new Congress, particularly as newly elected lawmakers might have limited knowledge of the country and its economic interests. 

Suggesting several key steps to improve prospects of securing support for Sri Lanka to get effectively engaged with the new Congress, he stressed the important of appointing a new Ambassador to Washington have an active diplomatic representation. 

“I think Mahinda Samarasinghe did a great job representing Sri Lanka and was very active in engaging both the executive branch and Capitol Hill,” he noted. 

Commending President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s efforts in addressing corruption, he said that he believes the new Democratic Congress was likely to scrutinise the human rights records of trading partners much more closely than the previous Congress did. 

He suggested some effective measures, including the repeal of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) as a priority, that the Government could improve its standing and strengthen its prospects for GSP eligibility.

“We have been talking about repealing of the PTA for 20 years since I was an ambassador there, and it’s long outlived its usefulness,” he said.

He added that repealing the legislation could also improve Sri Lanka’s prospects of securing the renewal of the European Union’s GSP Plus trade facility.

Blake further called for tangible progress on reconciliation, including the demilitarisation of the Northern and Eastern provinces, the return of seized land and steps towards the devolution of power.

“These are all longstanding issues that have been promised and shouldn’t be that difficult to do,” he said.

He noted that the Government had an opportunity to advance these measures while President Anura Kumara Dissanayake continued to enjoy significant parliamentary support.

Blake’s observations highlighted the importance of proactive diplomacy and progress on domestic policy issues as Sri Lanka prepares to engage with a new US Congress, where trade access and human rights could receive greater attention.

Sri Lanka under scrutiny

Former Foreign Secretary and Sri Lankan Ambassador to the United States Ravinatha Aryasinha explained the changing US political landscape from Sri Lanka’s foreign policy and economic perspectives.

He said Sri Lanka had significantly recalibrated its foreign policy following the 2022 economic crisis, moving towards a more balanced position that enabled it to maintain constructive relations with major powers.

Aryasinha, who is the Executive Director of the Regional Centre for Strategic Studies, stressed the importance of preserving the diplomatic space created through this approach, particularly as Sri Lanka approaches the conclusion of its current International Monetary Fund (IMF) program in March 2027.

“From a Sri Lankan perspective, I would think that we should try to hold on at least to that window we opened on foreign policy,” he said.

He noted that international stakeholders had supported Sri Lanka’s economic stabilisation partly because of their economic and strategic interests in the country.

According to Aryasinha trade, investment and regional security as three major areas requiring careful attention in managing relations with Washington.

Commenting on trade, he expressed concern over relatively flat growth in Sri Lanka’s exports to the United States, citing uncertainty surrounding Trump’s tariff policies, the absence of a trade agreement and potentially weaker consumer demand in Western markets.

He observed that Sri Lanka’s apparel industry had remained competitive primarily because of the quality of its products rather than preferential trade arrangements. 

“Sri Lankan apparel manufacturers compete successfully because they produce good-quality products. However, if tariffs increase or consumers reduce their purchases, the quality of the products alone will not be enough. This is something we need to watch closely and try to protect,” he said.

Ambassador Aryasinha acknowledged that attracting substantial foreign direct investment had remained a longstanding challenge, even during favourable economic periods.

He identified China’s established presence in Sri Lanka as a strategic consideration in US investment decisions but cautioned Washington against allowing its competition with Beijing to constrain engagement with Colombo.

“I am not telling the US that they must ignore their red lines,” he said, adding that demanding exclusive strategic alignment from Sri Lanka would be counterproductive.

He argued that Sri Lanka’s refusal to pursue exclusivity had helped maintain more balanced relationships with both Washington and New Delhi.

Aryasinha also referred to the regional implications of tensions involving Iran and the wider Middle East, stressing that Sri Lanka should retain the flexibility to make decisions based on its national interests.

He said the changing composition of the US Congress could bring renewed emphasis on human rights, reconciliation and democratic governance in Washington’s relations with Sri Lanka.

While acknowledging the importance of addressing these concerns meaningfully, he cautioned against using human rights as an instrument of political pressure.

Having served as Sri Lanka’s Ambassador in Geneva from 2012 to 2018, Aryasinha said human rights were used more as a means of keeping Sri Lanka under scrutiny. 

“The US did not provide us with offensive weapons, but it did provide intelligence, the war would probably have continued for many more years,” he commended the US assistance during the final stages of Sri Lanka’s ar. 

Despite differences over human rights, Aryasinha noted that bilateral relations had remained relatively stable through difficult periods. 

He said Sri Lanka had so far managed the changing international environment without suffering major diplomatic setbacks, although it might not have secured all the gains it could have achieved.

Concluding his remarks, he stressed that Sri Lanka should remain responsive to US concerns while expecting the US to recognise the importance of Sri Lanka’s independent decision-making.

“Sri Lanka does best when it is allowed to kind of come to these decisions on its own,” he said.

Questions over US regional policy

Henry Stimson Centre Senior fellow in the South Asia program Dr. Daniel S. Markey, explained on the wider implications of the US election outcome for South Asia, particularly Washington’s relationships with India and Pakistan and its approach towards China and the Indo-Pacific.

He described the Democratic gains as a significant political setback for the Trump administration, although he cautioned against interpreting the results as an outright rejection of its foreign policy.

“The best way to say where we stand right now is that we feel to be at the beginning of the end of the Trump era,” Dr. Markey said, noting that President Trump would nevertheless retain considerable executive power during the remaining two years of his term. 

For Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal, Markey said the future of relations with Washington would depend heavily on the strength of American diplomatic and government institutions rather than solely on decisions taken by the White House.

“The principal area of concern with dealing with the United States is process and institutions,” Dr. Markey, whose expertise are mainly focused on international relations and U.S. policy in Asia, said.

He highlighted the importance of professional diplomats and officials in the State Department, Defence Department and National Security Council in sustaining regional cooperation.

Markey questioned whether Washington would return to a more institutionalised approach to international relations or continue with a more personalised and transactional foreign policy.

Commenting on India-US relations, he said the election outcome was likely to be viewed positively in New Delhi, particularly following two years of friction over trade, the Iran war, Russia and Washington’s relations with Pakistan.

“The elections for India will in general terms be perceived as a welcome development,” he said.

Despite political differences, Markey observed that defence and technology cooperation between the two countries had continued through established government-level dialogues, military exercises and private-sector engagement.

He said the incoming Congress could provide further support for this cooperation.

However, Washington’s changing approach towards China remained a major concern for India.

Markey noted that for nearly two decades, US policy towards the Indo-Pacific had been shaped partly by strategic competition with China, making India an important regional partner.

“India was perceived by Washington as being very important, sometimes of principal importance,” he said.

He observed that the Trump administration had appeared to move away from this approach at various points, raising questions about Washington’s long-term commitment to the Indo-Pacific.

“None of these things provide the same confidence about U.S. commitment to its place of global leadership and especially not its commitment to the Indo-Pacific,” he said.

Dr. Markey said the next US administration could take a different direction on trade, alliances, climate change and multilateral cooperation, although a complete return to the Biden administration’s approach should not be assumed. 

The webinar provided an opportunity to exchange views on how the changing political landscape in the United States could influence international relations and the strategic and economic environment of South Asia.

In a match where dropped catches took the limelight, Sri Lanka Women squeezed through to a four-run win against Pakistan Women to end the Super Sixes round unbeaten and enter the final of the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy.

In their final Super Sixes match played at Karwan SC cricket ground, Ajman yesterday, Sri Lanka scored 140-6 and kept Pakistan down to a total of 136-9. But the highlight of the match was the appalling catching by both teams. Pakistan dropped four catches that allowed Sri Lanka to reach their total. In their turn, Sri Lankan fielders went one better by spilling five.

Sri Lanka had already booked their place in the final before this game. For Pakistan it was important for them to win to keep them in contention for a place in the final. But unfortunately for them they fell short of it.

Thus it was left to the Super Sixes match between Ireland and Netherlands to decide who the second finalists was going to be. Ireland came up with a strong batting performance to hit up 162-3 and defeat Ireland (118) by 44 runs to finish second in the Super Six standings to Sri Lanka (10 points) with 6 points.

Despite their poor catching Pakistan were able to peg Sri Lanka down to a reachable total through their bowling unit which was disciplined and accurate. Sri Lanka failed to get any big partnerships going in their innings. Vishmi Gunaratne, their in-form batter made 30 off 23 balls (2 fours, 1 six). 

It was her lowest score in the competition. Imesha Dulani held the rather inconsistent Sri Lankan batting to see her team reach a defendable total by contributing a stroke-filled half century – 56 off 38 balls (5 fours, 2 sixes), an innings that won her the Player of the Match award.

Pakistan got off to a dreadful start losing both openers by the second over and by the end of the first powerplay had lost four for 29. Omaima Sohail scoring at virtually a run a ball looked good for her 36 before she was run out. Tuba Hassan made 24 off 18, but it was the lusty hitting of Tasmia Rubab – 23* off 11 (3 sixes) that nearly clinched the match for Pakistan.

Seamer Sathya Sandeepani and left-arm spinner Sugandika Kumari took five wickets between them to deny Pakistan the win.

Europe finished with 299 runs across the boys’ and girls’ innings, with both sides contributing to the winning margin under the tournament’s Parity Rule. The boys earned a 21-run lead before the girls stretched it to 154 and held Matthew Hayden’s Australasia to 90-6.

Put in to bat, Europe’s boys raced to 52 without loss, with Shiv Ratna Shreyas striking 5 sixes in his 24-ball 40. Chirag Singla removed both openers and Gitarth Gupta struck twice in the tenth over as Europe slipped to 93-6 in the 15th.

Dhruv Shrikant Pise gave Australasia a head start in reply, hitting 7 fours and 4 sixes in a 26-ball 60 before Shreyas had him caught by Rohan. Ibrahim Khan made 22 and Arnav Kumar added 21, but Australasia finished on 145-7. Europe used 10 bowlers, with Rohan taking 2/37.

Pearl Muthamma B made 34 off 44 balls and Sophie Louise Warrilow scored a run a ball 31, but Australasia struggled to find runs against a European attack that sent down more than half the innings without conceding a run off the bat or in extras. Europe had previously finished ahead of AB de Villiers’ Sub-Saharan Africa on aggregate, only to draw under the tournament’s Conditional Draw Rule.
